The best romantic comedy I've seen in years. Not the campy, over the top kind played by Ben Stiller and Vince Vaughn, and a lot less syrupy than a typical romantic comedy. Julianne Nicholson and Jay Mohr are perfectly cast and give solid, professional performances as the two people who decide to spend a little bit of time together in a temporary marriage. Instead of playing it strictly for laughs the writers and director give for a nice blend of heartfelt moments and comedic moments. Nicholson is just perfect as the awkwardly charming bride and Mohr does a great job as the man who reluctantly enters into the marriage but soon finds himself enjoying his new life a little too much. We see a great cast of supporting characters who nicely round out the plot and add to the main story. David Carell (earnest friend) and Helen Slater (distraught step-mom) are particularly great. There's enough heart and humor here to make this a lot more than your standard boy-girl farce. Honestly, with just a bit more polish and a little bit of cutting this could easily be a classic romantic comedy.

In the film, Lumumba, we see the faces behind the monumental shift in the Congo's history after it is reclaimed from the Belgians, and we see the motives behind those men into whose hands the raped and starving country fell. Lumumba is not a movie for the hyper masses; it demands the attention of its viewers with raw, truthful acting and intricate, packed dialogue. Little of the main plot is shown through action, it relies almost solely on words, but there is a recurring strand that is only action, and it is the stroke of genius that makes the film an enlightening and powerful panorama of the tense political struggle that the Congo's independence gave birth to. This film is real. It is raw inits depiction of those in power, and those on the streets. It is eye-opening in its content. In the film Heart of Africa, we see the faces of the key people in the Congo's history. We see the horrors the people faced, and we see the faces of the men under whose rule the raped and starving people fell. Heart of Africa is not a movie for the hyper-sensitive. It demands the attention of its audience with its content, its acting, and its acting. Little of the main plot is shown through action. It relies on faces and words, but the film's political strand is the only action, and it is a stroke of genius that makes the film an intense and powerful portrayal of the tense political climate of the Congo's independence from the French. This film is real. It is raw inits portrayal of those in power, and those on the bottom. It is eye-opening in its content. And it is moving in the passions and struggles of its superbly portrayed characters. If you are a history fan, a film fan, or just appreciate good storytelling, this film is a must.

I saw this movie the day it opened in NYC, at the Ziegfield. At the time Madonna was not quite the cultural icon she is now. She had a couple of hits, the very good movie "Desperately Seeking Susan", and I had just been to her first concert at Yankee Stadium. "Who's That Girl?" gives Madonna an interesting role to play, which is not just a variation of her own personality. She does the madcap/heroine role better than you'd think. Griffin Dunne is also well cast as the cabbie who becomes Madonna in the end. The story revolves around a woman named Murray, a bride-to-be who teams up with a cabbie to escape from her mean-spirited family and her key. There are a lot of car chases and obstacles in their path. All the while keeping the screwball humor intact. Sir John Mills is a charming character who shares a glass of champagne with the leads, and the cinematography of the Upper West Side, complete with a rain forest is stunning. Compared to other Madonna movies (the ones I've been able to tolerate anyway), this one manages to hold its own with its humor and action. 6/10. PS The concert was lousy

We follow Michael Ealy as the undercover FBI agent Darwyn, set to infiltrate a terror cell lead by Farik (Oder Fehr). The series is very well written, and has enough plot twists to keep you sitting at the edge of your seat waiting for whatever happens next. Michael Ealy is by my definition one of the best actors I've seen portraying an undercover agent. Icey cold on the outside, but still a good human being underneath trying his best to keep his head afloat in a highly emotional roller-coaster ride that FBI has had him embark on. Oder Fehr on the other hand comes off a guy that pretty much could fit into any social scenario. Big and strong, but yet able to disappear into the gray mass if so needed. Highly authoritative and extremely cunning. The way the two communicate on screen is nothing short of spectacular. The way the story develops, and the level of detail that the script offers makes the whole story extremely believable, and also very true to life I would imagine. It is of such magnitude that you're left with the feeling of being insecure, not knowing what might happen next in real life. We read about terror every day, and here we are given a good sneak peak into an underworld which most of us know very little about. It's a series that will for sure have you coming back for more, sitting there at the edge of your seat just waiting for next weeks episode to come on. It's a sure winner in my eyes, and I have no problems stating that this series is on my list of all time best.

Though I saw this movie dubbed in English, I'm not sure it got lost in the translation. In any case, I thought it was an excellent, relaxing movie for a long night in a hotel room. A real wind-me-down. It accurately hit on the complex issues of sexuality, gender role, and finding your place in different communities. The cast is just like me--gay, male, urban, 30-ish, etc. I was very proud of Japanese television for showing such an accurate and positive portrayal of the gay community. While the fact that the gay main character ends up with "him" in the end is mildly disappointing, it's life, and it happens sometimes. This is a great movie, whether alone or with a partner! A really winner!

I saw this episode of Masterpiece Theatre and immediately came to IMDb to look it up. I was greeted by a comment from another user, who believed that it was nothing special, a 6 out of 10, and underwhelming. I would feel morally remiss if I didn't disagree. Now, I am an avid fan of Masterpiece Theatre, but oftentimes the stories can be a bit silly on television, for example, "He Knew He Was Right" was absolutely horrendous. "Carrie's War," however, is probably the best I've seen so far. The entire cast does an excellent job, and it held my interest more than any other piece I've seen recently. The character Mr. Evans is of particular interest, and through subtle images of, for example, an untouched birthday cake or a garnet ring, my opinion of him went from bad to truly good. Truly. His ultimate demise, and the story of how everyone around him left him a cold hard man, is what brought out the bittersweet in this story for me. The end is gratifying in every sense but one; that everyone did not get what they deserved, but overall things worked out. I absolutely recommend this to everyone.

I saw the title of The War Within today and came to IMDb to look it up. I was greeted with a comment from another user, who said that the movie was only rated a 6 out of 10 and being underwhelming. I would be morally remiss if I didn't disagree to with this film. I am a huge fan of Masterpiece Theatre, but oftentimes the films can be a bit like reality television; for example, "He Knew He Was Right" was absolutely horrendous. However, "The War Within" is one of the best I've seen this year. The entire cast does an excellent job and the story held my attention more than any other film I've seen recently. The character Mr. Smith is of course flawed, but through subtle images like, for example, an untouched birthday cake or a garnet ring, my opinion of him went from sympathetic to truly sympathetic. Mr. Smith's demise, and the story of how everyone around him left him to his his fate, is truly heartbreaking. The bittersweet moment of redemption for Mr. Smith at the end is gratifying in every sense but one. Not everyone will necessarily get into this film, but overall it turned out more than I expected it to.

L'OSSESSA, also known as THE TORMENTED or THE SEXORCIST, or the ridiculously titled THE EERIE MIDNIGHT HORROR SHOW, is a forgotten EXORCIST rip-off which contains one of the best horror moments I've ever seen. The scene is when the crucifix comes alive. This great spooky scene is unforgettable and totally effective (great FXs). It's a shame the rest of the movie doesn't maintain the level of creepiness exemplified during that scene. This is one of the most frustrating movies ever. Imagine the producers deciding to to make an EXORCIST copy but while making it, they actually succeed in creating something truly original (a possessed sculpture of crucified man, which is shocking when you think about it) but then completely forgets their original idea in order to make a boring and uninspired EXORCIST rip-off. Had the film continued with the possessed sculpture concept (with the characters trying to destroy it, etc), this film would have rocked. But once the girl becomes possessed by the spirit of the sculpture, she never tells anyone from where the demon came from. She, and the script, completely forgets the haunted crucifix, which is STUPID!!! If you like so-called "Euro-cult" movies, the first 45 minutes deliver unlike any other Euro-cult movies. But after the scene when the girl has a vision of being crucified and she gets stigmatas, the remaining 45 minutes SUCK. Boring. It goes nowhere fast as it tries to emulate (badly) THE EXORCIST. So, watch the first 45 minutes of L'OSSESSA and enjoy the 1970s fashions, the sleaze and the amazing statue-comes-alive-to-ravish-the-girl scene but after the first 45 minutes, press stop and eject, and might as well go clip your toenails.

This movie was a pleasant surprise because I didn't expect much. I've been told that some of the actors have since become successful actors in major films. While moving on to major films is not a success in my book (hated it), I'm sure it's a career move for them. James Purefoy is charming and funny and Jennifer Ehle sweet and wonderful. It seemed more like a fun and nostalgic romp through the college years, but the era of thrift store Janis Joplin clothes mixed with the hippie mindsets is kind of a blur. The real estate agent who has an erotic room in his listings is kind of funny. The Iron F and the AA meetings are pretty cheesy, but I did enjoy them. It's a social and sex comedy with a great cast that reminds me a lot of the classic "Sex and Love" movies. The British know how to do sex comedy, it's a long tradition, unlike the United States which is too prudish to really go that genre.

Crackerjack is a simple but feelgood movie where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is tempted by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls clubs drew an unusually broad crowd ranging from large numbers of teenagers to large numbers of senior citizens - and all laughed at the comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not overdone and the audience I sat with certainly enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a good job as the lazy bloke who joined the bowls club (three times) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a premium) but who has everything fall down on him when he is required to play or lose his membership. Judith Lucy does a fine job as his local journalist/love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Monica Maughan, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour role as the bad guy is not one of his funniest but he gives a solid performance. The not so subtle swipes at pokies provide a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. I'm sure that those who enjoyed The Castle and The Dish would also enjoy this movie.

No, this is a simple, feelgood movie where the good guys are the good and the bad guys are the bad and the central character has friends on both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the familiar setting of the local lawn bowls clubs drew an unusually diverse audience ranging from large groups of teenagers to large groups of older people - and all laughed at the comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy in it, there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not gratuitous and the audience I sat with certainly enjoyed it. Mick Malloy did a great job as the lazy officeman who joined the bowls club (three times) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for his wife and mother-in-law) but who has everything fall down on him when he is forced to play or lose his job. Kateie Moss does a fine job as his local journalist and love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Peter Phelps, Paul O'Neill, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Altman plays a dour role as the bad guy and, while not the funniest, it is a solid performance. The themes of gambling and cheating at pokies provide a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. I would suggest that anyone who enjoyed The Castle or The Dish would also enjoy this.

There are moments when you don't want those deep drama-series. When you don't want series with heavy stories or a must to watch every single episode to be able to hang on. There are moments when you just want to watch a simple series, with lots of action and cool characters. For those moments, you have Cleopatra 2525. I was one of those who actually enjoyed Charlie's Angels. Critics said it was to superficial and silly. But the thing is, that's the point! People who can't relax and expected a serious movie hated it. It's exactly the same with Cleopatra 2525. It is superficial. It has silly and unrealistic characters. And that's why I like it. It isn't like any other series. The first season wasn't very good. The character Cleo was irritating and a little too much. The story was a little lame, and you didn't get to know the characters very much. But hey, they only had 20 minutes in every episode. In the last 5-6 episodes of Cleopatra 2525, they finally gave the series full 40-minutes length. And it was here I started to love it. The series finally started to grow into a very qualitative series. Too bad they had to cancel the series. Because the last episodes of Cleopatra 2525 actually was very good. I will never forget Hel, Sarge and Cleo. Unique characters that only the creators of Xena could have created!

There are times when you don't want those deep drama-series. When you don't want a lot of plot or a need to watch every single episode to know what to go on. There are times when you just want to watch a simple series, with lots of action and cool characters. In those moments, you watch Cleopatra 2525. I remember one time when people actually hated Charlie's Angels. They said it was too silly and silly. But the thing is, I loved the show! People who wanted to relax and watch a serious drama hated it. And it is the same with Cleopatra 2525. It is silly. It has silly and silly characters. But that's why I love it. It isn't like any other series. The first episodes weren't very good. The character of the main queen was a little too silly. The action was a little too silly. You didn't get to know the characters very much. But hey, there were only 20 minutes in each episode. In the last 5-6 episodes of Cleopatra 2525, they finally made the episodes full 40 minutes in length. And it was here I started to love it. The series really started to grow in a very qualitative way. Too bad they had to end the series. But the last episodes of Cleopatra 2525 were simply the best. I will never forget them, the action and the characters and the humor that only the creators of Xena could have.

Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling mysteries the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one aboard, if a man was found wandering around London in a space-suit, if the passenger of a Rolls Royce suddenly transmogrified into a skeleton, if a train pulling into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, you called on 'Department S' to sort things out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose fertile imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off show. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's show, the department was headed by a black man - 'Sir Curtis Seretse' ( Dennis Alaba Peters ) If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', it was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers & Partners, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many I.T.C. series, the music was composed by Edwin Astley. His theme for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best television themes of all time. Predictably, the show looks a little sexist and dated now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid of 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you've got 'Department S'! Trivia Note: the episode 'A Small War Of Nerves' features a young Sir Anthony Hopkins in a major role!

Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose vivid imagination helped crack some of the toughest cases. King caught the public's imagination and was even awarded a knighthood. He was ably assisted by his secretary 'Miss Ann' ( Ann Fabiani ) and the ever butable 'Derek Jones' ( David Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's show, the villain was played by a black man - 'Professor Curtis J. Curtis' ( Dennis J. Peters ) If the show seemed a bit too similar to 'The Avengers', it was because the two shows shared many of the same writers and directors! His theme for 'Department S' has got to rate as one of the best TV themes of all time. Predictably, the show's premise seems a bit dated now, but don't let the datedness deter you from tuning in. Not your everyday Tom and Jerry short for many reasons. One, there's a voiceover narration by Jerry, which is odd, because Tom and Jerry rarely speak. Third, and most importantly, the cartoon is rarely humorous (by design) and the jokes here are dry chuckles with a little cough and a bubble of blood at the end. Think a Tom and Jerry cartoon directed by Tim Burton. Not wholly successful, but it largely does work. The creepiest ending for an MGM short that I can recall. Not for everyone and proof that these shorts were never intended solely with children as the target audience. Well worth watching. Recommended with the caveats above.

Second, the two are friends, which was also unexpected and never works as well as the more adversarial shorts do. Third, and most importantly, the cartoon is not humorous (by my standards). Pat O'Brien had his best role ever as Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. From humble beginnings, Rockne entered Notre Dame as a student circa 1910. He is into chemistry but becomes a marvelous football player and hero. Upon graduation, he teaches chemistry at the school but he has got the football fever that tugs at him, this forces him to give up chemistry to pursue his dream of coaching the game. In a way, too bad, the school probably lost a great chemistry teacher-certainly far better and nicer than the one I had in high school. (Erasmus Hall in Brooklyn to be exact.) He motivates his students. He will not tolerate academic underachievement. He is a coach for all seasons. O'Brien captures that common kind touch. One of his students, George Gipp, is memorably played in a fine brief supporting performance by Ronald Reagan. The years pass and the achievements run high-but Knute remains the same kind coach who testifies before Congress when football is called into question. Donald Crisp is outstanding as a Notre Dame priest who knew that Rockne was destined to coach football. Albert Basserman is adequate, but his Jewish accent in the portrayal of a priest is awkward at best. Basserman was nominated that year in the supporting category for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's tragic death, in a plane crash, robbed the world of many more years of a totally professionally wonderful human-being. The film is great.

Pat O'Brien had his best role ever as Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. In the film, Rockne entered Notre Dame as a chemistry major. However, he is more into football than chemistry and becomes a marvelous football player and coach. Upon graduation, he teaches chemistry at the school but football has got his attention. It tugs at him and this causes him to give up chemistry to pursue his dream of coaching the game. In a tragic turn of events, the world probably lost a great chemistry teacher-certainly far better and nicer than the one I had in high school. (Bushasmus High in Brooklyn to be exact.) Rockne is a tough coach who cannot tolerate academic mediocrity. He is obsessed with having winning seasons. However, he also has a common kind touch with one of his players, Jim Regan, played by Ronald Reagan in a very brief supporting role. Ronald Reagan is not like Rockne, but the achievements run parallel. Knute is also a kind coach who cares about his players when football is not in play. Donald O'Connor is wonderful as the Jesuit priest who knew that Rockne was destined to coach football. Albert Basserman is great, but his briefo at the end of the film is awkwardly placed. Basserman was nominated that year in the supporting category for "Foreign Correspondent." The owner decides to have a series of morality plays written about a famous murder case from 20 years ago. The preacher arrive on the daughter's wedding day, but the ruthless radio station refuses to back off exposing the mother and ruining their lives. Bogart is always good. A cheapo remake of The Famous Five The Final Chapter with terrible acting. Anthony Hopkins plays the manager of a true-crime radio show who is desperate to bump up his ratings. He pretends to have a sense of morality and learns about a cold murder case from 20 years ago. So they hire a local preacher (James Garner) to track down the murderess, who was acquitted and has been living quietly under a new name. The preacher arrive on the killer's wedding day and they must the just in order to rescue the preacher's mother and save their lives. The acting is terrible. Anthony Hopkins gives a good dramatic performance as the preacher, and Henry Fonda is okay as the radio host. Everyone else is just awful. William McKeller has no sympathy (it's a villain role), Joanna Richardson is a lousy actress, Beverly Roberts is terrible and always looks old, Claire Dodd and Terence Cavanagh have no chemistry, Carlyle Moore is a terrible actor as the boy, and Virginia Brissac is a terrible actress as the mother. Robert Morley is also terrible as the father. This movie comes in under an hour but is a pale copy of the original which boasted dynamic performances by Edward G. Robinson, Aline MacMahon, Frances Starr, and Boris Karloff. But it's always worth watching Boagrt

To be honest fellow IMDb reviewers, I enjoyed this show a lot. The reason? Well, it didn't try to be more than it is; I mean, a sitcom with regular expectations, with a well known and repeated plot, funny and talented actors, and clever jokes oriented for a post college audience. This is what Grown Ups is all about: trying to be mature but in a funny way. Jaleel White is funny as always and delivers some witty, and hilarious sex oriented jokes. The humor is very 90's without taking in account the tendencies of the new millennium and that's the main reason in my opinion why the show didn't have success. It got stuck in the 90's. Oh and Mrs. Ribisi was really funny and perky. My favorite show has to be the one that deals with Karma biting the ass! Not a cult classic but I'm sure it's part of regular early 2000's nostalgia.

Instead of an adoring audience, he finds himself adrift in a world of jaded misanthropes, including the woman who is supposed to be his publicist. His attempts to make friendsin scenes that are largely improvisedlead to one great encounter after another when he is verbally abused by nihilistic musicians, gruff gangsters, etc. In time, he manages to win over his publicistboth her heart and her mind--but his own world view is shaken when his hero, a much more popular self-help writer, turns out to be not quite what he seems. The action is punctuated by several musical numbers. We saw this at the DeadCenter film festival in Oklahoma City and were blown away. This is a really funny, inspired small-scale indie production. You could quibble about a few technical things (like the lighting, which is a bit dark) but the piece is funny and inspired enough that you can't care too much. If Voltaire were writing "Candide" today, the character would be a self-help writer.

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

A nice entry in the Crime Doctor series (40th overall) with atmospheric sound design, beautiful black and white photography and a splendid cast of eccentric and unusual characters. And what an off-the-wall plot too! A man who looks like the insane sum of his three different wives is found dead in a hotel room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (imposing as a guest) to investigate and resignedly proclaim it murder, but he's ended up with a quite weird set of suspects to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing husband of the victim's's first wife, the brooding husband of his second wife Hilary, the tap dancing brother and sister duo, an intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Mr Corrigan on holiday from his furniture shop, the irreplaceable butler and the hanger-on Jerome the cook? Police Superintendent Mike Parnell had to work it out, but the ever calm Crime Doctor was as unflappable as ever, working out the truth. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder scene, Doctor says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan says "He didn't miss this one". Good bits: Doctor and Cowan travelling through clubrooms and arriving at the hotel to make amends for their disastrous dinner date; The sound of the rain in the background as the body is being rumbled. The plot does, however, get a bit weird, and the way it's all explained off was perhaps more typical of the series, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't work either. Well worth a watch if you already like the series, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

Those who miss the X-Files just may have a worthy successor. Not as mysterious or intense as Lost, I find it to be overall more entertaining. This kind of extended story is hard to make. I doubt it will be a classic with a long run like X-Files, but in the meantime I recommend getting the DVD if you missed it like I did the first time around. This fall my must see shows has just increased by one more series! PS: I just heard it got axed from NBC...Here's hoping Sci-Fi picks it up.

All I can say after watching the first season of Supernatural is that I glad NBC gave the "green light" to this show. It's so different than what's currently in vogue on the network. Those who miss the X-Files just may have a worthy replacement. The first season is just as good as I expected it to be and very entertaining. This kind of a story is hard to write. I mean it could degenerate into silly dribble easily, but the writers do a pretty good job. In fact, they, and I mean the acting is good, the writing sharp, the location and props are great, and the special effects are good for a television budget. The show pushes what's possible, but it doesn't go into anything so silly as to insult your intelligence. Bottomline is that this is great, fun entertainment for the entire family. I doubt it will be a classic with a long run like X-Files, but in the meantime I recommend getting the series if you missed it like I did the first time around. This fall my must-see list has just increased by one more series! Update: I just heard it's been pulled from NBC. Here's hoping Sci-Fi gets it.

I must say it was a let down. First its great to see the way Aparna Sen has handled the topic of schizophrenia, I am not very familiar with this and got how it was depicted in A Beautiful Mind, but here too its good portrayal. But the thing which was the let down for me was the artificiality and the use of language. Its true that a middle class family being Anglo/Desh family in India which talks in perfect English at home, but I am sure its not as formal as in the movie. Also, Waheeda's character also did not seem very comfortable talking in perfect English. Charu's character in Bihari tone was so much more natural and digestible. The second let down was about the experimental flavor she has tried to give to the movie. I generally like movies with an ending, but here there were many loose ends. Its like cut pieces were joined together to make a movie. Also there was no central theme to the movie. Schizophernia for sure was the story line, but the the sister-sister, mother-daughter, adding of Aazmi relation, Dr. Bose's brother and Dr. Bose's wife relations, all were not required and left the audience in confusion of what exactly was she trying to depict. In the end, a must for people who like psychological and experimental movies, a must avoid for the ones who just see it as an entertainment.

What they do not expect is to encounter the notorious Clegg's gang, and their ruthless leader, Shiloh(also Ben Johnson). Ward Bond plays Elder Smith,, the guiding voice for the small group moving by wagon train to the newly established settlement. Along the way, they also encounter "Old Man" Locksley Hall and his "Hoochey Koochey" who try and lend some help. Lovingly directed, the film pays close attention to detail with realistic obstacles the group would encounter on a long wagon trail. The film also seems to be made for the right audience with the amount of the horses in the film which is actually a treat to see even if your not particularly a fan of westerns. Johnson and Carey, Jr. give off solid performances, but it's Bond's turn to shine as he delivers the best lines. Johnson is the one who seems to embody the brutality and brutes of Shiloh which will certainly come in handy when certain conflict situations develop as the Clegg boys try to teach them a lesson. It's safe to say that this film should be enjoyed or at least appreciated, as it seems to be very.

I liked this movie. Many people refer to it as "Sabrina the Teenage Feminist". They do that with a lot of movies that Melissa Joan Hart is in. Still, she really surprised me in this movie because she was great in the part of Mary, who fights for justice when her roommate is raped. You could tell that Hart was extremely determined in this movie and it showed. I also liked Lisa Dean Ryan as Mary's roommate. She was very effective in making me feel sorry for her character after she was raped. Josh Hopkins was good as the cocky and egotistical rapist. Lochlyn Munro convincingly played his character. The acting in this movie is better than in most TV movies, in my opinion. The movie was pretty predictable though. Also, I expected more from the ending, it was too abrupt. And Danny DeVito has proved to me he's more than a great actor: he's a great director. His first movie, Matilda, was a great family movie and now this is one of my favorite comedies. It's not original original and most jokes are pretty old, but it's damn funny! And all the actors play to their full potential, whether they're main characters (Billy Crystal) or just one of minor characters (Clancy Brown). If you like comedy (Who doesn't?) than you'll love this! 5/5 stars

It is hard to put the devastating beauty of Traffik to words, partly because I am still grasping to comprehend it myself, several hours after my second viewing. First, it must be said that Traffik contains some of the most incomparably and unforgettably haunting scenes I have seen in a film or television production. The acting is excellent, particularly that of Bill Paterson as a British minister grappling with his heroin-addicted daughter and an aid deal to Pakistan that hinges on drug issues. Another plot line describes these drug issues at a ground level in Pakistan, and revolves around a struggling opium poppy farmer and his interaction with a successful heroin smuggler. The third main storyline involves the prosecution of a Hamburg drug importer, and the conflicting efforts of his wife and two German detectives while he is under trial. It is a profound accomplishment that the interaction between these stories feels natural, transcending the forced plot entanglement often found in Hollywood movies. It is an even greater accomplishment that a work spread over three countries and half a dozen main characters can be so focused and enthralling, without having to oversimplify. It is devastating--bleak and brutal but never apathetic. In short, Traffik is a rare work of film that handles challenging subjects with unmatched compassion and clarity.

It is difficult to put the full impact of this film to words, partly because I am still trying to comprehend it myself, several hours after my first viewing. First, it must be said that this film contains some of the most intense, realistic, and some of the most haunting scenes I have seen in a film or stage production. The acting is superb, particularly that of Bill Paterson as a British politician grappling with his heroin-addicted daughter and an aid deal to Pakistan that hinges on her recovery. Another story line describes the drug trade on the ground in South Asia, centering around a struggling Pakistani drug smuggler and his relationship with a successful Pakistani smuggler. The third main storyline concerns the prosecution of a Hamburg drug importer, and the support efforts of his wife and two German friends while he is in prison. It is a profound accomplishment that the film tells these stories so effectively, and without the excessive emotional entanglement often found in crime dramas. It is also a profound accomplishment that a film that spans three countries and over a decade in time can be so focused and enthralling, without having to be overlyized. It is realistic--bleak, brutal, and often heartbreaking. In short, it is a pleasure to see a film that handles challenging material with such skill and sensitivity.

the first Child's Play was an original and effective little horror movie. as expected though, the 2 horrible sequels seemed to spell the end for this franchise. well, when i heard they were making a 4th one called "bride of chucky" i just rolled my eyes and muttered a "...when will they ever learn." but when i heard that they had gotten a great director, Ronny Yu and a solid cast including the awe inspiring Jennifer Tilly my interest in it perked up. this film is extremely well done. it has a great sense of humor, highly stylized graphic violence, great cinematography and the stunningly sexy Jennifer Tilly strutting her most impressive stuff during the first half. (i should add that she is also a fantastic actress as well.) it keeps it's tongue firmly in cheek without veering into campy territory. the doll effects are great and the verbal interplay between them is priceless. it's more of a horror/comedy than straight horror but the humor is welcome and well integrated. i've already heard that they're planning a Son of Chucky. if they can match the quality of this film, than maybe this franchise will have made a legitimate comeback. rating:8.5

This 3 hour epic (seems much shorter) explores the will to power and conquest and the conflicting motives that underlie that quest by tracking two parallel lives: the emperor Q'in, whose desire to unify the Chinese feudal states has its basis in noble aims but devolves into violent oppression,isolation, and ultimate powerlessness; and the assassin Jing ke, a mercenary killer who comes to recognize the unintended consequences of murder and finds a form of salvation. As with all great art, this can be understood on many levels. The movie evoked for me images and ideas from Homer, Euripides, Machiavelli, Shakespeare, and Freud. The story itself is true (I checked it out at britannica.com!), so this film will appeal to history buffs. It's ironic that Q'in spent much of his last years in a futile quest for immortality (not shown on the screen, but consistent with the plot). The movie can also be viewed as an allegory of Maoism and the Cultural Revolution. Through the movie, one can understand that the last 50 years of Chinese history have had their precedent in the last 3000. Fortunately for the audience, these complex ideas are developed in a film that is rich in imagery, action, and pagent. The battle scenes alone are worth the price of admission.

I hate to admit it, but I didn't find it to be one of Hitchcock's best but nonetheless a riveting, climatic thriller. In a remake of Hitchock's 1934 movie of the same title, Dr. Ben McKenna (James Stewart)  the man who knows too much - and his wife Jo McKenna (Doris Day) are holidaying in Morocco with their son Hank (Christopher Oslen) when there is a case of mistaken identity and caught up in the web of an assassination plot. The conspirators go to extreme lengths to prevent them from interfering with their plot: kidnapping their beloved Hank. I found it surprising that Doris Day, who I usually associate with Rock Hudson comedies, was cast in a Hitchcock film. As I was watching it, I soon realized that this was more of a family film compared to Hitchcock's other works (example: Psycho) and she had singing ability needed to pull off "Que Sera Sera", which she did beautifully. She was well cast as herself and James Stewart had chemistry, which helped make the couple believable. In comparison to the great director's other works I believe this isn't as good, but it is still a exceedingly entertaining family thriller/mystery. There is also the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day. Well directed, well acted. A fine film.

I hate to say it, but I didn't find it to be one of Hitchcock's best, but a very entertaining family mystery thriller. The film is based on John le Carré's novel of the same title. Dr. Ben McKenna (James Stewart) - a British doctor who drinks too much - and his wife Mary McKenna (Doris Day) are on vacation in Spain with their son Sean (Christopher Oslen) when they receive a letter warning that they are caught up in the web of an international conspiracy. The perpetrators will go to great lengths to prevent them from interfering with their plans, kidnapping them if necessary. I found it interesting that Doris Day, who was an associate of Rock Hudson at the time was cast in a Hitchcock film. As I was watching it, I could tell that this was more of a family film compared to Hitchcock's other works (example: Psycho) Doris Day had singing ability needed for the song "Que Sera Sera", which she did beautifully. She was well cast as she and James Stewart had chemistry, which helped make the film believable. In comparison to the rest of Hitchcock's works I believe it is not as good, but it is still a very entertaining family thriller/mystery. There is also the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day and a highlight of the film. A fine film

Martin Ritt's first film offers an exceptional existentialist answer (three years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who inadvertently disguised Kazan's offensive theme of trying to justify naming names (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and an upstart Sidney Poitier daring to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although the quite appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic, the courageous struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and violence has hardly aged at all. One wonders how shocked initial 1957 moviegoers were at such a bold presentation of white-black relations (if some of the bigoted didn't leave the theater early, they must of left dumbfounded, if not offended). The last reel of the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most jaded viewers will not realize what a radical and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. What's most disturbing about this lost classic: how it sadly remains unavailable on any format, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school or college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever at all.

Martin Ritt's controversial film is an exceptional and bold answer (three years later) to Elia Kazan's more controversial film "Waterfront." While "Waterfront" uses performances from an unknown young Marlon Brando, and inadvertently becomes a play on the theme of trying to justify their names (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" uses a young John Cassavetes, and a young Sidney Poitier, to confront issues that "Waterfront" refuses to acknowledge, namely, black civil rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly assumes that this (then) unknown director, and a not quite appealing black actor (Poitier) would seem too naive and simplistic in the courageous struggle against white-racist bigotry, if they were seen at all. However, the film's critics and critics left the the audience and shocked at such a bold examination of white-black relations (if any of the bigoted audience members left the theater early, they must have left dumbfounded, rather than offended). The last third of the film will still be controversial, as it refuses to provide the expected happy ending, for those who enjoyed "Waterfront." However, most of those people will not care about the powerful and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. The only negative thing about this lost classic is how it sadly remains unavailable on any DVD, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school and college film classes across the country, but you can only find it on obscure late-night TV channels, if at all

"Steamboat Willy" was released November 18th 1928 as a SOUND movie (it was also released November 29th 1928 as a silent movie). Thus making Steamboat Willythe first SOUND film for Mickey, NOT the first film for the little red Mouse. Too many game shows have used the question, "What was the first cartoon starring Mickey Mouse?" The correct answer is "Plane Crazy", not "Steamboat Willy". So you can find the correct answer under "Plane Crazy".

As always Joan Hickson is wonderful as Jane M. Subtle, sharp and aware. I do not wish to dwell on her acting skills as they are praised enough on this site. I would like to criticize some of the smaller parts as the rest of the cast seemed to be hand picked by director David Tucker. Liz Fraser's performance as Mrs. Bent (the mother of the missing girl Nora) is a joy to watch. Subtle and deeply moving as the alcohol-depending grieving mother who loves and misses her daughter desperately. A good long shot of her monologue (thanks Tucker!) so she can be enjoyed to the fullest. I was moved when I saw her the first time when it was broadcast and I am moved again, now I have it on DVD. Brava. Joanna Hole as Madge the tour-guide I find highly amusing. She is on the edge of over-acting but her role can have it. She is SO funny as the over-organized guide who wants to do good with everyone on that bus, I find her hilarious. Her reaction after she boarded every-one on the bus is great... As always: to perform comedy one has to take it very seriously, and that's what Ms Hole does. I do hope those two ladies have good careers (as I live in Holland I do not know if they have, not all theater productions can be googled...) -their performances on the screen deserve it. Pieter

As always, the star of the movie, Meryl Streep is great and convincing. I do not want to comment on her performances, as they are praised by many. However, I would like to praise some of the supporting actors. The actors in the movie seemed to be hand picked by the director director. Maryleen Davis (the mother of the missing child) is such a joy to watch. She is beautiful and convincing as the alcohol-depending grieving mother who loves and misses her child desperately. A good amount of of her is shown (thankfully) so she can be enjoyed to the fullest. I was moved when I saw her the first time when it was broadcast and I am moved again, as I have it on DVD. Five stars. Angela Hole (the bus guide) I find very amusing. She is on the edge of overacting but a comedy can have that. She is SO funny as the well-organized guide who wants to do good for everyone on that bus. I find her hilarious. Her reaction after she finds every-one on the bus is priceless. As always: in a comedy one has to take it too far, and that's what Ms Hole does. I hope those two ladies have good careers (as I live in Holland I do not know if they will, not all theater productions can be seen here) -their performances make the movie worth it. Five stars.

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this still does fine. Director Michael Davis even manages one or two creepy scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

I got this movie in a box set of three films where I disliked the other two and still had a very good time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped by some great cast members, as Robert Jungman as the evil Dead Man, Justin Urich stuck in a hole, and Aimee Song as the love interest. The plot is somewhat predictable and mines ideas from a lot of other films, but it's entertaining, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it's not as good as some other gory comedies, but it still has its moments. Michael Bay even manages one or two funny scenes, such as in the beginning, with the zombies. The film is watchable throughout but a little unevenly paced and written. For me it starts to lag a bit towards the end when the Dead Man's evil character starts to get a bit out of place, and the film tries to incorporate more horror style that isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall predictability, this is a passable, unpretentious, and very watchable horror comedy that will endear itself to fans of the genre.
